Yet, the original approach struggles to handle anisotropic data sets containing both essential and insignificant dimensions. Due to its uniform treatment of all dimensions, the method is prone to noise from non-informative dimensions, leading to suboptimal performance. Furthermore, the existing search space is too vast, making synthesis computationally infeasible for large problems. Our research builds upon the original work, presenting a semi-decididable criterion for combinatory logic-based synthesis and proposing an optimization technique to reduce the search space based on dimension importance. Through practical synthesis tasks, we show that identifying unproductive dimensions can significantly condense the search space, from exponential to polynomial complexity. We also develop a practical synthesis algorithm leveraging the optimized search space, demonstrating a notable improvement in synthesis time. Specifically, our approach facilitates the synthesis of efficient logical circuits for data with significant dimensions from large and complex datasets, such as data centered around the (2+2)-fold, resulting in rapid and feasible computation. Moreover, we show that combinatorial logic-based synthesis can efficiently handle high-dimensional data sets even with multiple significant dimensions. Notably, our approach allows the direct transformation of anisotropic data into optimized logical expressions, reducing synthesis time from hours to seconds or even real-time. Ultimately, our technique maintains little overhead, as the additional computational cost is just 3.2 times the original synthesis time. We consider our approach a flexible and generic solution, as it can apply to various other high-dimensional data sets in further research. By synthesizing efficient logical expressions from multi-dimensional data sets, we reveal the dimension-dependent optimization as a future research direction, achieving reduced synthesis time from hours to seconds or real-time. Consequently, we facilitate the direct transformation of anisotropic data into optimized logical expressions, rather than requiring data transformation as in previous approaches, thus maintaining little overhead, at a cost of just 3.2 times the original synthesis time. We believe this work to be a foundational step towards further research, as it presents a generic synthesis technique and leaves dimension-dependent optimization for future investigation. By achieving real-time synthesis, we demonstrate the feasibility of direct logical expression generation from multi-dimensional data sets. To investigate this phenomenon further, we conducted a series of experiments transposing the general neural network learning algorithm onto a complex system of brick-like particles arranged in a dense 2D and 3D structure. For dense prediction tasks like super-resolution, even the highest-end graphics cards are often insufficient, resulting in the use of image slicing or tiling techniques which leads to uneven processing and decreased overall performance. Our proposed solution, DeepVR, tackles this issue by transforming super-resolution into a series of image resizing jobs that can be processed in parallel across multiple images, thus turning the problem into a distributed computation with multiple input images. This job splitting approach, coupled with automatic job scheduling using priority queuing, enables efficient handling of varying sized jobs that result from processing super-resolution models of different complexity levels. Our platform also ensures that there is always a high-performance model available for each job by utilizing a pre-trained model cache and incorporating on-the-fly model quantization techniques. Our evaluation on the DS3K video dataset demonstrates that DeepVR surpasses the super-resolution performance of multiple benchmark models, including PSNR and FID, when compared to a single high-performance model and further shows little to no quality loss when compared to a high-performance model in terms of SSIM when deep quantization is applied.   **Title:** Efficient NAS Evaluation based on Early Model Sampling

  **Abstract:** 

  Early model sampling is a technique that allows for the evaluation of neural architecture search algorithms before reaching the end of the pre-defined search budget. In this study, we employed late arrival and early termination strategies to apply this technique. Firstly, we used flaky neurons to prune sub-networks at regular intervals, resulting in multiple candidate models per training epoch. Secondly, we applied a ranking-based early termination strategy to stop search trials with under-performing models. Our experimental results reveal that this approach significantly reduces computation costs while maintaining accurate model accuracy predictions. Moreover, we found that combining early model sampling with data augmentation transforms NAS into a task that can be accomplished within an hour on modern computers. The paper also discusses the implications of our discoveries for the development of efficient NAS evaluation procedures. Lastly, we found that our NAS evaluation framework yields a versatile set of models that exhibit strong performance in downstream tasks. This is consistent with the behavior of our SE-PRUNER search algorithm, which was used to generate these models.

Our investigation focuses on the narrow line Seyfert galaxy, FEGC049, which exhibits significant UV and UV variability similar to that of LBVs, as well as narrow emission lines. By analyzing OWLS data covering 11 years and multiple space telescope observations, we find that FEGC049's UV flux appears to follow a power law distribution with an index of 2.2, which is in agreement with the prediction of the reverberation mapping technique and is consistent with the galaxy's continuum being produced by hot stars. Furthermore, we observe that FEGC049's UV flux exhibits correlated variability with a time lag of approximately 42 days when compared to H-beta reverberation mapping, which is remarkably similar to the time lag seen in the 1850s periastron observations of the supermassive binary system Beta Lyrae. Despite this, we present evidence suggesting that FEGC049 is unlikely to be a classical LBV due to the absence of emission lines with high velocities as well as striations on the continuum and Ia supernovae candidates. The origin and nature of FEGC049's UV variability is still unknown, but it's possible that it's caused by hot stars moving through the galaxy's dust cloud or a combination of effects including wind interaction and stochastic mass loss. FEGC049 challenges the existing paradigm that low mass LBVs primarily exhibit moderate and long term variability, which may need to be revised if it's confirmed to be an LBV. FEGC049's UV variability makes it an attractive target for future studies of the galaxy's emission lines and structures down to 0.1 Angstroms, which could provide insights into its complex wind and variable star nature. The analysis presented in this investigation also highlights the significance of continued, long term UV and optical monitoring of FEGC049 as well as other LBVs and narrow line Seyfert galaxies in order to further understand their shared and distinct characteristics. Finally, we suggest that FEGC049 be classified as a variable star of a previously unrecognized type which is likely related to the broader LBV category, which is given the name superstructure LBV. The unique properties and potential variability of the superstructure LBV class is an area that requires further investigation and study. The data that supports the analysis presented in this investigation is publicly available online. \\

Adaptive trials, using Bayesian methods to determine dose levels, can switch to a higher dose if preliminary results indicate a better safety profile, thereby optimizing trial efficiency. However, selecting the optimal starting dose is still a challenge, particularly in cases where limited information is available from previous studies. Experts then use predictive distribution of the Bayesian model's parameters or the model itself to make informed decisions. A technique we propose involves utilizing the predictive distribution of the Bayesian model to calculate the probability that the Maximum Predictive Accuracy (MPA) criterion will be satisfied at a given starting dose. This approach is then verified using simulations for two popular likelihood functions: the logistic and the Probit models. Finally, a comparison is made between the performance of both models in terms of trial efficiency, defined as the ratio of the required Type-I Error to the probability of exceeding the MPA criterion at various starting doses. Our findings indicate that the Probit model surpasses the logistic model in terms of trial efficiency, particularly at higher dose levels. Therefore, adapting the Probit model in clinical trials can significantly enhance trial efficiency, ultimately accelerating the development of new drugs. Furthermore, our proposed statistical method provides accurate predictions, thereby enabling better decision-making when limited information is available from previous studies. Lastly, our research reveals that the Probit model's efficiency can be further improved by selecting a starting dose level that is relatively far from the Maximum Tolerated Dose. Thus, incorporating the Probit model into clinical trial designs can result in substantial time savings. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for the use of adaptive Bayesian designs in clinical trials. Additionally, our research can be extended to include complex models featuring moderate and high model complexity, feature selection, non-linear regression, and using neural networks, among other possibilities. Finally, our simulation studies demonstrate that the Probit model's performance can be compromised due to the presence of outliers, suggesting the need for effective outlier removal techniques in clinical trials. Furthermore, four related topics have been proposed as potential articles for other statistical journals. (OD) data in natural language processes is a crucial evaluation method for understanding how well to train a model. Unlike traditional assessments, this method doesn't rely on expert-labeled samples but instead uses natural language expressions to define OD categories. We examine two leading OD detection approaches and adapt them to categorize context-free OD expressions within text. We evaluate these models using a newly created dataset that includes OD expressions from various natural language benchmarks. The results show that both models perform effectively on detecting OD expressions, with one model exhibiting stronger matching abilities and the other exhibiting stronger contextual understanding. We discover that combining their predictions leads to improved accuracy within a supervised setting. However, in an unsupervised setting, the model exhibiting stronger contextual understanding often produces lower-quality results by incorporating irrelevant context, according to two proposed evaluation metrics. We propose an alternative training strategy that encourages the model to match strings by reducing the penalty for non-categorical matches and increasing the reward for categorical matches. The proposed training strategy and two evaluation metrics are available at https://github.com/rohan-joshi/od_detection_for_context_free_expressions. We anticipate that these contributions will facilitate future research on OD expression detection and related topics within natural language processes.

  A key challenge is that the methods used to train RL policies and value functions are often sensitive to outliers in the data.
  These anomalies, which can result from both noisy experience collection and intentional manipulation, can significantly
  skew the model's training, leading to poor generalization and making the model vulnerable to data poisoning attacks.
  Current solutions focus primarily on training RL models to maximize performance on the compromised dataset, which does
  not guarantee that the models will perform well on the true reward function in the absence of the malicious data.
  In this work, which was inspired by the threat model proposed by Li et al. for gradient-based machine learning, we show
  that specific forms of malicious data can be transferred directly to the true reward function by training RL models to
  minimize a loss function tailored to the compromised dataset.
  To illustrate this finding, we implemented a dataset of PGG game experience that contains two types of malicious data
  designed to transfer to the true reward function, which we used to train robust offline RL models using both decision-based
  and value-based methods.
  Our experimental evaluations, which considered multiple types of malicious data transfer triggers, demonstrate that the
  models we trained were significantly more resistant to data poisoning attacks in the true reward function compared to
  standard offline RL models. In fact, our decision-based model achieved a 135% relative gain in performance when exposed
  to an attack on the compromised dataset, while also retaining near-optimal performance on the compromised dataset itself. 
  Our work establishes key limitations and challenges, however, including the lack of data availability, which could hinder
  the applicability and validity of our findings. Furthermore, the fact that the forms of malicious data transfer that we were
  able to detect are relatively simple suggests that the effectiveness of our methods may be vulnerable to more sophisticated
  approaches in the future. Finally, our experimental evaluations were labor-intensive to conduct, which could make it difficult
  to apply our methods across a wide range of RL domains. Future research will aim to address these limitations by developing
  more general data poisoning attacks, expanding beyond decision-based and value-based methods, and investigating the
  feasibility of applying our approach to more complex RL environments. Ultimately, our goal is to develop robust offline RL
  models that can effectively mitigate data poisoning attacks in the true reward function. 
  The code for our research is available at https://github.com/krishnanlab/

The Blumofe queue is a concurrent data structure designed to facilitate efficient execution of multiple tasks in parallel, with proven performance optimization capabilities. However, its complex operational logic poses significant difficulties in terms of linearizability, a key concurrent system property. To resolve this issue, we developed a proof of linearizability for the Blumofe queue using an automated reasoning tool called TinyMC, which generates and proves correctness evidence for the queue's implementation. The success of this proof demonstrates the efficacy of TinyMC in verifying complex concurrent data structures, even with complex operational logic. This verification proof also showcases the practical relevance of TinyMC, which can effectively analyze real-world concurrent algorithms. Additionally, we formally state and prove a new theorem, which states that any correctly implemented queue will be linearizable. This new theorem, known as "queue linearizability," serves as a valuable tool for verifying queue implementations, significantly simplifying the process of checking linearizability for certain queues, including the Blumofe queue. By combining this new theorem with TinyMC, we successfully reprove the linearizability of the Blumofe queue, achieving this proof through a more straightforward and efficient reasoning process. This entire verification process, including the proof of queue linearizability, has been formally documented and made publicly available. This work marks the first successful use of TinyMC to verify the linearizability of a complex concurrent data structure, which will enable us to explore further optimizations and improvements in concurrent algorithm design. Finally, we outline promising research areas, which include the application of queue linearizability to other complex data structures and the use of TinyMC to verify real-world operating systems, as well as concurrent algorithm performance optimization through machine-learning based validation and identification of inefficient paths in concurrent execution logic. Overall, this work aims to showcase the practical utility and ground-breaking potential of TinyMC in verifying and improving the linearizability of complex concurrent data structures and their impact on performance. have electric charge 0 and are assumed to couple equally to all standard model

possible. We aim to identify experimental signs that could indicate the
occurrence of such $Z'$ hadronic leptons at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). 
Specifically, we examine the influence of $Z'$ hadronic leptons on the following

they may be verified or disproven through ongoing and future LHC experiments.

experiments are applied to find the $Z'$ hadronic lepton mass range; (II) the
correlation between $Z'$ hadronic lepton production and the standard model
processes at the LHC is examined, and (III) the distinct features of $Z'$ hadronic
leptons at future LHC experiments are compared with those of standard model

  Among various types of imaging data, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) stands out due to its non-invasive nature, high detail resolution, and multi-modal capabilities. As a result, there is an ever-growing need for processing large sets of MRI data, which often encompasses analyzing one or multiple MRI scans in three-dimensional space over time.

  The goal of this task is to identify the leftmost cardiac ventricle in each MRI scan. This aim is closely related to a broader objective known as cardiac structure extraction, which involves defining the boundaries of ventricle regions within the three-dimensional space of an MRI scan.

  To accomplish this task, we suggest an improved iterative method for selecting landmark points. This proposed method incorporates two key techniques: initial boundary estimation and boundary refinement.

  For the purpose of this discussion, we will use the term "slice" to refer to a two-dimensional cross-section of an MRI scan, and "axis" will denote a direction in three-dimensional space. Based on these definitions, our method consists of the following steps:

  1. Determine initial slice positions: We will discuss how to select the initial boundary iteratively, beginning with slices that contain notable landmark points. Once the initial positions are established, we will discuss how to update them based on previously acquired data.

  2. Refine iterative results: After calculating the new slice positions, we will discuss how to update the boundary refinement over time, ultimately leading to the final selection of the leftmost cardiac ventricle.

  Through our proposed model, we have achieved significant accuracy when compared to other methods, particularly in multiple-sequence MRI scans. Our approach is characterized by its simplicity, making it easy to understand and implement in a variety of settings. Ultimately, our model provides high-quality results, surpassing many other techniques in terms of accuracy and performance. 

  The code for this project is available at https://github.com/whereisjoe/tree-mri-analysis. We present this work in detail in a paper titled "An Improved Iterative Method for Selecting landmark Points in MRI Data: An Application in Cardiac Structure Extraction."

Since predicting the price of an artwork solely based on its value is impossible, the task is considered challenging. Training models using human-annotated price and visual features is unfeasible due to the scarcity of priced images. As such, publicly available datasets on artwork pricing are rare. 

  The study proposes an innovative solution to determine the price of an artwork based on the probability of selling it at a specific price during an auction. This approach relies on a probability distribution, not a fixed price, which accommodates uncertainty associated with estimating the artwork's value. As a case study, the methodology is applied and evaluated on the 'Masterpieces' dataset, containing information on 21,689 artworks sold at auction along with their visual features and category attributes. The experimental design includes comparative analysis of prediction methods, focusing on the effectiveness of leveraging visual features, category attributes, and their combination in determining the probability distribution of the artwork's price. 

  The results indicate that a combination of visual features and category attributes yields the best performance. Moreover, the probability distribution of the artwork's price provides accurate predictions, surpassing the performance of models predicting a fixed price. Finally, the methodology is validated through experiments on two separate evaluation metrics, demonstrating its capability to differentiate between various artist profiles and determine their impact on the probability distribution of the artwork's price. 

  The study's findings reveal that artist profile has a statistically significant influence on price determination in the art auction market. Notably, certain prominent artists, such as Picasso and Monet, experience lower price drops over time and more frequent sales compared to other artists. Additionally, similar styles, such as Impressionism and Expressionism, exhibit distinct price trends and characteristics that can aid in price prediction in the art auction market. 

  The study's ultimate goal is to provide insight into the complex art auction market, offering valuable knowledge that can be utilized by artists, galleries, and auction houses to influence and navigate price fluctuations in the market. By addressing the challenge of predicting probability distributions of the artwork's price instead of a fixed price, the methodology can contribute more significantly to their fields, ultimately providing accurate insights into price determination.  The proposed methodology can be applied to various fields where valued items can be sold at auctions, such as antiques and collectibles, and where predicting probability distributions can be more informative than predicting fixed prices.

This study reexamines the origin of the observed imbalance between IMFs in localized areas and those predicted by theoretical models, focusing on two factors: magnetic fields and collisions between supersonic stellar outflows. Using magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we investigate the impact of varying magnetic fields on the fragmentation of rotating gas clouds. When the magnetic field reaches a critical level, it prevents the cloud from fragmenting into multiple stars, replacing it with a single more massive star. In such scenarios, optimising performance may require prioritising correlations over accurate signals.  Here, a simple Bayesian model is adapted using data augmentation to transform the scenario into one where correlations take precedence. Ultimately, we propose an even broader conjecture, C$_{\mathcal{M}}$, which encompasses the previous KQ-conjecture as a special case, and show that it is true for the specific structure of model-theoretic classes with the local infinitary logic property, L$_{\kappa,\lambda}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the validity of C$_{\mathcal{M}}$ in this broader context would imply the feasibility of finding a proof of the infinitary version of Elliot's theorem, which is considered a more fundamental goal within the field of model theory. The structure of our paper, including the organization of $\S\S 1-2$, mirrors the content, as noted in the introduction. We present the main results in $\S\S 3-5$ and then summarize the key outcomes in $\S 6$. Lastly, we include an appendix collecting auxiliary proofs

pandemic's global spread have been fueled by debates over the effectiveness of lockdowns and the significance of daily case numbers.  In an effort to clarify these discussions, we investigate the coronavirus's evolution within small populations of susceptible and infectious individuals, taking into consideration lockdowns' impact on social interactions.  By combining theoretical epidemic models with simulation-driven analytical tools and examining the long-term behavior of these systems, we find that: (a) for large populations, the epidemic will eventually die out; (b) for extremely small populations, the coronavirus may not be wiped out; (c) models that account for average social interactions align with case number patterns seen in real-world data; (d) models that incorporate variable social interactions align with both case number and death number patterns seen in real-world data.  Given our findings, we suggest that average social infection models are more suitable for long-term analysis of coronavirus epidemic dynamics and that variable infection models are more effective for short-term forecasting.  Additionally, we provide data-driven estimates for the pandemic's early stage and simulated data for comparison with current vaccination efforts.  Our research provides scientific understanding that can help inform the public health measures and evaluation methods of the coronavirus pandemic.  Our code and other materials are publicly accessible at https://github.com/roushanizadeh/effective-coronavirus-epidemic-models.  We have also published a related paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07167, both of which can be accessed for free.  We intend for these resources to contribute to further research in this field.  We believe that accurately modeling the coronavirus pandemic can help inform the critical decisions of governments and health authorities that are still grappling with infection dynamics and the effectiveness of public health measures.  We also recognize that accurate modeling is ongoing and models should be updated as new data becomes available, which is why we are openly sharing our work and encouraging others to contribute.  We hope that our study inspires research in this field and that our findings and software benefit scientists who are working on infection dynamics and the critical challenges of public health. Despite advances in higher organisms, models of ion channels for larger squids have been largely overlooked. Their giant axons, similar to other squids, have relatively simple characteristics, making them ideal for channel modeling. By using electrophysiological techniques on intact fibers from the giant squid, our paper presents measurements of key properties associated with the fast and slow voltage-gated potassium channels. The results include current records, activation and inhibition velocity, and conductance levels for both channels. These properties are in line with previous studies on single channels in cell-attached configurations. Our data, however, reports a higher than expected slow potassium channel conductance, suggesting a simpler structure for these channels. Our findings can help refine computational models of ion channels for squids, which exhibit rapid and persistent hyperpolarization due to a unique type of potassium current. This trait is beneficial for squid swimmers who use fast and prolonged hyperpolarization to enhance their movement efficiency. Furthermore, the large size of the giant squid axon makes it an excellent model for understanding ion channels in larger cells of living organisms. By studying this model, researchers can gain insight into various cellular processes and conditions, such as epilepsy, where abnormal and prolonged hyperpolarization has been observed in neurons. Lastly, our data can help resolve any discrepancies between previous experimental data and the available biophysical models of ion channels. Our results may also be useful for various advanced modeling techniques, such as molecular dynamics and Markovian models of ion channels. Nevertheless, a substantial gap remains in the development of methods effectively counteracting noise amplified by iterative attacks. This issue is crucial because repetitive adversarial perturbations frequently result in significantly distorted data, making them nearly impossible for models to resist. As an attempt to bridge this disparity, we propose an innovative framework, the reversible predictive network, which incorporates a versatile module for tackling complex noise. This framework's module is capable of removing multiple types of noise patterns while predicting the direction and speed of the temporal adversarial perturbation gradient flow. Moreover, we integrated this module into state-of-the-art reversible architectures and significantly improved their ability to resist adversarial perturbations, particularly in scenarios of high iteration contamination. Our experiment results demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing approaches, further, the code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/reversible-prediction-network.   Our paper delves into adversarial perturbation amplification and proposes a pioneering framework known as the Reversible Predictive Network (RPN). Comprising a module capable of reversing and predicting contamination patterns and adversarial perturbation gradients, RPN significantly boosts a model's resilience to repeated adversarial attacks. This framework's module can learn the high-dimensional amplification patterns of various contaminants without needing explicit matching signals. As demonstrated in our experiments, our method strongly outperforms adversarial training, overcomes multiple contaminants without being tailored to each one, and significantly surpasses models without predictive capabilities. Our work is the first to address predictive reversal and provides comprehensive evaluations on a wide range of datasets, including ImageNet. Our code is available on https://github.com/zwang84/reversible-prediction-network. This research was supported by NSF grant number 1925194, with additional resources from the University of Nebraska - Lincoln. We would like to extend our gratitude to Qian Chen for her contribution in this research.

By incorporating the principles of dependently typed programming, we can develop a blockchain framework that incorporates both immutable data structures and formalized program correctness, thereby reducing the need for additional cryptographic measures. This is particularly challenging using current quantum devices, which have low error thresholds. One effective method involves using Reichardt's error correction protocol, taking into consideration the varying errors that can occur when measuring qubits. By assuming a limited diversity of errors, we have found an efficient way to run this protocol within a predictable amount of time, thereby enabling the use of such error correction techniques on large-scale quantum devices even when individual qubits have very low reliability. This concept was formally proven using bounded-degree bi-regularity, a method of tackling problems in graph theory. By showing that the required memory and steps needed to run the protocol are proportional to the number of qubits and the inverse of the error threshold, we have established an important criterion for assessing the practical use of such error correction codes in various computing systems. One key aspect of our proof involves presenting an error correction code that uses a specific pattern to eliminate errors, allowing it to achieve a lower bound of error elimination based on the degree of the code's graph. By applying bi-regularity, we have also found a way to transform any given code into a more suitable 'bi-regular code' that meets certain criteria and has a higher level of error elimination. We have demonstrated the feasibility of such bi-regular codes by proving that a code with a specific type of error elimination, known as $((\frac{2}{3}+\delta)^n$, can be transformed into an error-free code using a specific pattern, known as a 'cycle code', when $\delta$ is greater than zero but less than one-third. We have shown that the required steps needed to do this are proportional to the cube of the number of qubits and that such codes can eliminate errors with a rate of nearly one, meaning that the majority of the code can be directly utilized for computing tasks. We have also applied this concept to data storage, finding specific conditions under which bi-regular codes can be used to reliably store data on a scale proportional to the number of qubits. We have further extended this concept within a broader framework, encouraging future research on the controlled elimination of qubit errors, including the ability to monitor and act on individual qubits. Determining the precise impact of aerosols on climate remains a challenge and requires comprehensive modeling that accounts for the interplay between aerosols and clouds. This study incorporates a detailed representation of aerosol dynamics within a large-scale climate model to analyze the interaction between aerosols and clouds. By simulating radiative effects similar to observed climate patterns, our model exhibits realistic aerosol indirect effects on cloud albedo and atmospheric water content. The modeled climate impact of aerosols corresponds to a cloud longwave radiative effect of -0.23 W/m^2 and a total shortwave radiative effect of 1.76 W/m^2, aligning with estimates from Large Eddy Simulations and global climate models. Our model shows that aerosol indirect effects reach their maximum at a particulate nitrogen feedback elasticity of about 10% per unit ratio of cloud water to total aerosol, with observable variations in humidity levels and cloud types. A key issue in this area is the need for efficient separate channel recovery (SCR) methods that extract original signals from channel outputs with interference. {Na_2}$ and $\mathrm{K_2}$ in particular, are characterized by a rich electronic structure that features several valence electrons and diverse bond types.  The complex electronic physics of these systems is a result of the interaction between valence electrons with their potential coupled state.  The presence of an ion core poses a significant challenge to describe the system's electronic structure accurately.  To address this issue, we employed a recently developed ionized coupled-cluster methodology, based on the one-electron coupled-cluster model, for the study of $\mathrm{Na_2}$ and $\mathrm{K_2}$.  Our CCSDT-1pN3 corrections allowed us to evaluate up to third-order electronic correlations, encompassing single, double, triple, and triple excitations combined with non-covalent one-electron effects.  Through CCSDT-1pN3 corrections based on the complete active space perturbation theory, we were able to incorporate active space perturbations up to third order.  Results from these corrections were applied to the 1$\mathrm{^1\pi\sigma}$ and 2$\mathrm{^1\Sigma_g}$ states of $\mathrm{Na_2}$ and the 1$\mathrm{^3\Sigma_g^-}$ state of $\mathrm{K_2}$.  Our findings indicate that energy corrections for $\mathrm{Na_2}$ are sufficient at the CCSDT-1pN3 level, exceeding CCSDT-related total corrections.  In contrast, higher-order ionized excitations contribute negligibly to energy corrections for $\mathrm{K_2}$.  The accurate treatment of high-excitation regions through CCSDT-1pN3 corrections for valence regions, coupled with an effective ion-core description, enables the resolution of complex electronic physics issues related to coupled states and near-degenerate states.  This advancement is particularly significant for photoionization studies, allowing the accurate computation of ionized electron amplitudes and photoionization cross-sections even in systems with diverse electronic structures and coupled states.  The incorporation of further high-excitation corrections, coupled with total corrections based on high-excitation coupled-cluster models, may further enhance the accuracy of these results. Certain bound state spectra in QCD can be continued analytically to complex planes containing poles corresponding to quark and anti-quark states. Our investigation reveals that bound state spectra generally do not have this analytic continuity property. As a result, spectrum information derived from lattice QCD that appears to exhibit a simple, orderly pattern may indicate the presence of quark model states that also exhibit such a property. In contrast, bound states consisting of different quarks may also exhibit this property under specific conditions. This finding has significant implications for the existence of solutions in certain fractional elliptic and parabolic equations, and it also bridges the gap between nonlocal and local partial differential equations. Specifically, it provides a methodical approach to the study of perturbed nonlocal elliptic and parabolic equations. Primarily, our methods build on the work of Fefferman and Steiner, who established that any Lipschitz domain in R^n can be softened while maintaining consistency with trace operators. Finally, we examine the perturbed fractional elliptic and parabolic equations using the 'extension-traction' approach, and we establish a crucial comparison theorem for perturbed fractional elliptic equations. This paper proposes a novel approach called WiFi positioning by trace matching (WPTM) that eliminates the need for a pre-built database, thereby simplifying the process of collecting and updating data. WPTM compares newly collected WiFi traces with existing ones in a database, allowing for object location determination. To improve accuracy, this method aggregates the matches with the highest probabilities, thereby achieving higher positional accuracy. Simulation results in a real-world environment demonstrate the efficacy of WPTM, yielding an average error of less than 2 meters. After testing and validating this model, the results show an average positional error of under 2 meters. Importantly, the marginal loss can be adjusted according to the desired positional accuracy, thereby allowing us to achieve even lower error rates. Compared to traditional WiFi positioning methods, WPTM presents a number of simplified algorithms, namely LSH, MC, and CMC. Research on metric spaces has been extensively growing. To further explore these spaces, a new generalized metric space model is proposed in this paper: T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces. Initially, the study focuses on complete T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces and then extends to those with a completion. Several key properties for these spaces have been established: convergence of Cauchy sequences, the existence of completions, and the uniqueness of the completion for T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces. By defining a metric on the completion, it is proven that the completion is indeed a closed subspace within the product space of T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces. Many theorems have been shown to be applicable for these spaces. Moreover, several important inequalities including Banach's, Borsuk's, and Minkowski's inequalities have been proven in the context of T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces. By extending the concept of contraction mappings to T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces, many interesting theorems have been derived. Lastly, it is proven that the completion of a T$_{\alpha}$-metric space is contractible. These results open up new avenues for research within the realm of T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces. By comparing T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces with other generalized metric space models, it is shown that they offer certain advantages. Consequently, it is proven that many important mathematical theories, including fixed point theory, can be extended to the completion of a T$_{\alpha}$-metric space. Many interesting theorems have been generated as a result. Eventually, it is found that T$_{\alpha}$-metric spaces are synonymous with b-metric spaces. As a result, many important inequalities, including Schwarz, P\'olya-Szeg\H{o), Jensen, and Faber-Copson inequalities, have been proven in the context of b-metric spaces. Furthermore, it is proven that the concepts of contraction mappings and Banach's fixed point theorem can be effectively applied to b-metric spaces. Lastly, it is found that b-metric spaces are equivalent to metric spaces, thus confirming many existing results. Ultimately, it is shown that the concepts of generalized metric spaces are mere representations of mathematical abstractions. Consequently, it is found that many important results can be derived from the simple principle of generalized metric spaces. Many interesting theorems have been generated as a result. Finally, it is shown that many important results can be applied to the completion of a metric space

Recent studies have shown that obfuscation attacks can significantly compromise the reliability of machine learning models by hiding data labels.  To counter this, our research proposes the first defense strategy for obfuscation attacks by incorporating a novel utility-driven unobfuscation module into the standard adversarial defense framework.  By analyzing various unobfuscation modules, our experiments demonstrate that a module incorporating difference-based utilities can effectively remove the influence of obfuscation on data labels and cooperatively work with existing adversarial defense strategies such as certification and quantization for accurate model prediction outcomes in scenarios with compromised input integrity.  Our research further establishes formal theoretical links between unobfuscation module performance, adversarial perturbation characteristics, and acceptable error margins in quantization, which provides a framework for selecting optimal unobfuscation module designs based on these factors.  With theoretical and experimental validation, our proposed framework can confidently address the challenge of model trust by providing a clear path from high-level objectives to the selection of practical module implementations.  Ultimately, our research opens the door for further exploration of the unobfuscation module, for example by incorporating learning-based designs, to enhance the overall performance of the utility-driven unobfuscation framework. By taking into account the effect of quantization after training, the influence of rounding is quantified, and upper bounds on error rates are derived based on properties of the network and the quantization methods used.  By applying these results to specific problems such as binary neural networks and vector of loaded (VOP) networks, the impact of quantization is further analyzed, and practical methods for improving model accuracy after training are provided.  These results show that certain deep network architectures can achieve nearly optimal error rates even when weights are restricted to low precision, and propose new benchmarks for binary neural networks.  Moreover, the paper suggests potential improvement strategies for these architectures, and provides a practical approach to refine the models' performance.  Numerous experiments validate the derived theoretical results, and demonstrate the proposed training methods with VOP and binary neural networks.  Interestingly, the best model architectures may not necessarily involve low-precision networks, but rather those with a higher capacity for handling quantization, which implies that achieving the best error rates often requires formalizing the quantization process.  In general, the work here extends the previous theoretical studies to a broader, more flexible hypothesis set, which in turn leads to better practical performance, and includes new experiments to verify the derived bounds, which show that quantization may degrade network performance but not as much as expected, and that certain architectures can handle quantization better than others.  Lastly, the paper includes a detailed analysis of the relationship between training and testing processes, which suggests the need to develop new methods for validating the learned models' properties, and potentially reduce the gap between training and testing error rates.  By opening up these broader challenges, the paper may facilitate future research in this area, and provide utility value to the existing theoretical framework.  Conversely, the quantization bias may now be a significant factor, which means that new validation methods could be necessary to ensure that learned models are accurate and generalize well.  Ultimately, the main contribution of this paper is the discovery of new theoretical tools and concepts, which can now be applied to other fields beyond deep neural networks, and specifically to the study of algorithms, which could benefit from similar analysis and generalization techniques. These systems can be affected by external forces or influence other systems in which case the dynamics are governed by a coupled Markov jump process. To analyze these interactions, we develop a framework for studying coupled Markov jump processes, which we leverage to investigate the conditions under which the process is irreducible, has a unique stationary distribution and is asymptotically stable. Our theory is applied to examine the effect of spatial correlations in a system of autoregressive random fields, revealing that the transition rates and system state significantly impact its stochastic behavior. Furthermore, by approximating the system, we show that the coupled process converges to a continuous-state Markov process as the transition rates approach infinity. Additionally, the coupled process is simulated to demonstrate that its spatial correlations vary greatly based on the system's configuration, with highly irreducible systems exhibiting extensive spatial correlations. Ultimately, the conditions that favor irreversible systems are identified through the measurement of system entropy in two distinct microstates. The coupled Markov jump process is utilized to model a system of autoregressive random fields with spatial correlations of varying degrees, where the state of the system is represented as microstates that are highly correlated with each other. To measure the irreducibility, a matrix is examined where the lower triangle of the matrix contains the transition rates from one microstate to another. A non-zero value in the matrix indicates the possibility of transitioning from one microstate to another, while a zero value restricts such a transition. Based on this matrix, systems that have a path to reach any microstate from another are considered irreducible. To analyze the existence of a unique stationary distribution, a detailed balance condition is examined for each system. Detailed balance requires that when one microstate transitions to another, the probability flow is conserved, ensuring the stability of the system. To investigate the conditions under which the system is asymptotically stable, a leaping technique is applied and shows that as the transition rates approach infinity, the system converges to a continuous-state Markov process. This process is characterized by a system configuration and a set of Poisson distributed variables that represent the occurrence frequency over time. The conditions for asymptotic stability are examined based on this new approach and shows that as the transition rates diverge, the system can no longer be in two distinct microstates and converges to a continuous-state Markov process. In this study, we address the challenge of developing a mapping between two parameterized function spaces that accommodates varying dimensional inputs and outputs.  Our approach is based on constructing a neural network that maps a low-dimensional input to a high-dimensional output while meeting specific criteria as defined by a variational method.  By formulating the problem within a high-dimensional space that encompasses both input and output dimensions, we use kernel ridge regression to generate constraints that the mapping must adhere to. Our method allows for the development of a neural network that maps a low-dimensional input to a high-dimensional output while adhering to specified properties. The current standard for BNN analysis involves assuming a specific prior distribution and analyzing posterior distributions, but this approach presents challenges in terms of understanding the complex interactions between individual models and their outputs. Learning complex recognition tasks through online self-improvement and incorporating prior knowledge about categories are crucial for both animals and machines.  Recent studies on biological visual recognition have made important discoveries and provided new insights into the commonalities and differences between biological and computer-based vision systems.  This review article examines recent breakthroughs in biological visual recognition, compares them to computer vision, and explores the shared principles and distinct characteristics of biological and computer-based vision. Compositional meaning theories generate the effect from the cause by applying a series of semantic functions to the premises of a sentence.  However, this approach often leads to problematic interpretations of sentences with multiple causes or those containing adverbs and adjectives that carry causal implications.  Despite these limitations, the cause-effect structure in natural language offers valuable insights into the underlying semantics of causality.  Inspired by systems in logic with built-in properties for reasoning about causality, we introduce Logics for the Causal Structure in Language (LCST), a comprehensive framework that evaluates and compares various logical systems for modeling the cause-effect structure in natural language.  LCST systematically examines and assesses eight logical systems, comprising both multimodal logical extensions and complex logics with built-in properties for causality, by applying them to a broad range of natural language phenomena involving the cause-effect structure, as documented in the Causal Atlas project.  The Causal Atlas is an extensive semantic resource that covers over 9,000 English sentence variants, systematically exploring the interactions between 57 causes and 41 effects across various domains of both everyday and technical significance.  By leveraging the Causal Atlas and eight logical systems for an exhaustive analysis of over 200 semantic phenomena involving the cause-effect structure, we identify the top candidates for modeling the cause-effect structure in natural language semantics.  The correlation between the interpretability of logical formulas and the cognitive biases present in human judgments reveals that people's interpretations of causally ambiguous sentences are influenced by both the explicit information provided and their pre-existing causal knowledge.  By integrating the results of human judgments with the interpretability of logical formulas, we identify the preferred logical system for modeling the cause-effect structure in natural language semantics.  The proposed system, causing, is a multimodal logic of the modal $\mu$-calculus with the least number of complex operators, and is now available as an online tool for reasoning about causality in natural language.  The integration of causing with other established NLP tools, and the application of online demos for causality in natural language, enforces the connection between the cause-effect structure in natural language semantics and the core cognitive biases that govern human causality reasoning.  The extensive resources, including the Causal Atlas, causing, and a tool for online reasoning about causality, are openly accessible for further research in automating the connection between the cause-effect structure in natural language semantics and the core cognitive biases that govern human causality reasoning

The research introduces protocols that enable committed parties to successfully decode messages despite interference from malicious agents, while ensuring the secrecy of transmitted data remains intact. The study invests heavily in analyzing the robust binary commitment problem at each stage, considering various parameters such as leakage in storage, processing, and reception. The results provide a comprehensive understanding of how much disturbance can occur before the commitment process fails. The findings also show that only certain types of malicious attacks can compromise the system, and the system's effectiveness is largely determined by a single parameter. The paper presents strategies to mitigate up to $p^{3/2}$ amount of noise in some scenarios and $p^2$ in others, while keeping transmission complexity at $O(n)$ for certain settings and $O(\log n)$ for others. The study demonstrates the existence of interactive protocols with specific properties, including independence of previous interactions and direct dependence on input data, in certain scenarios. The results provide a framework for achieving commitment with high levels of security, even with minimal interactions, by utilizing techniques such as list decoding and binary reconciliation. The paper provides a step-by-step algorithm to construct interactive protocols, and includes specific examples of successful systems in scenarios with up to $p^{3/2}$ noise and $p$ noise. The study shows that these protocols are not only highly secure but also achieve improved transmission efficiency, including a 50% reduction in transmission complexity in some scenarios. The results appear to be tight, as increasing the number of stages would allow for higher levels of noise reduction, though this comes at the cost of increased interaction and list decoding complexity. The paper presents a distinct paradigm for robust commitment, which involves achieving high security levels through multiple stages, even in scenarios with $p_{\rm ext}$ noise that exceeds the internal security parameter $p. The study demonstrates that these ext noise values can be as high as $p_{\rm ext} = \sqrt{p} + p$ with five stages, and $p_{\rm ext} = 3p$ with six stages, before the commitment process becomes non-uniform. produced by a cold, magnetized, gravitationally bound plasma in the vicinity of a black hole. This emission results from magnetic field fluctuations on a scale comparable to the Larmor radius, for electrons moving at 10-50 percent of the speed of light relative to the black hole. To quantify the emission intensity, we introduce the concept of'magneto-optical susceptibility.' By treating the synchrotron radiation as a generalized Compton process, we apply the framework of $T$-matrix calculations to derive an optical approach for predicting the emission spectrum. This approach enables us to simplify the computation and achieve two key outcomes: (1) the emission spectrum can be determined solely from the magnitude of the $T$-matrix, and (2) the frequency dependence of the emission spectrum can be separated from its polarization dependence. Applying this approach, we are able to predict the emission spectrum within a given polarization state, without employing a frequency-dependent plasma model, and obtain results in agreement with extensive particle-in-cell simulations. Furthermore, we identify three distinct regimes of emission, each corresponding to a particular phase of the magnetic field fluctuation, and find that the spectral hardness is directly proportional to the electron acceleration rate and inversely proportional to the plasma frequency. By integrating over all polarization states and relevant photon frequencies, we calculate the total synchrotron luminosity and find that it scales with the square of the electron acceleration rate and the third power of the Larmor frequency. Finally, we determine the upper bound of the total synchrotron luminosity as a function of the plasma frequency and find that it is significantly influenced by Doppler effects and non-relativistic corrections, though it may be surpassed by Doppler-scattered radiation when the electron energy is high. Overall, this work lays the foundation for future research into hard synchrotron radiation produced by plasma fluctuations, and the predicted relationships between spectral properties and plasma characteristics offer valuable insights into the characteristics of turbulent plasma in the vicinity of black holes. Additionally, the $T$-matrix approach and the magneto-optical susceptibility concept presented here may also be applicable to the study of synchrotron radiation in other intense astrophysical plasma systems. The EGY theory predicts that K-Y particle creation will occur in a black hole due to quantum fluctuations in the time-like direction for a rapidly moving observer. Using our approach, we attempt to observe this phenomenon by sending Gaussian light pulses through a section of nonlinear fiber and measuring their scattering off solitons produced by the Kerr nonlinearity. The first model assumes random occupation of the lattice sites by atoms, leading to distinct quantum states. By comparing theoretical predictions with experimental results from an actual experiment, we find that experimentally created quantum states significantly deviate from the theoretical model due to atomic diffusion across the lattice during the preparation process. Alternatively, we model the optical lattice as a closed system with a specific probability of atom transition between adjacent sites, enabling us to calculate the entire spectrum of possible quantum states. This model is consistent with the experimental findings, indicating that experimentally prepared quantum states are also part of a broader continuum. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that even though the initial mixture may appear "mixed," it can exhibit features characteristic of an isolated "pure" quantum state. Moreover, we analyze the boundary between mixing and measurement and discuss the potential for transitioning between these states by adjusting lattice parameters in experiments involving ultracold atoms. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of our model to other types of atomic experiments through an analysis of a three-dimensional optical trap containing a specific type of atom, known as $^{167}$Tb. This study contributes to the understanding of quantum state preparation in complex systems and provides a framework for experimenting with quantum simulations using ultracold atoms, allowing researchers to achieve specific goals while implementing various techniques. Our work also makes previously published results from experiment "One-dimensional quantum walk of ultracold atoms in an optical lattice" (arXiv:2101.11088) fully interpretable. Ultimately, we open up the potential for novel research in this field, including examining the influence of breaking symmetries in quantum state preparation and preparing pure quantum states through adiabatic methods in experiments involving ultracold atoms. This study has been submitted for publication in Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics and is currently available on arXiv as an in press article (arXiv:2103.16611). Furthermore, we have an accompanying experimental study (arXiv:2006.12694), which has been accepted for publication in Physical Review Letters, describing the practical application of our theoretical model through ultracold atom experiments. When complete, these papers will contribute to the understanding of quantum state preparation in complex systems in physics, as well as provide valuable practical knowledge in this field. Lastly, we have an accompanying video explaining the motivation and methodology of our work (available at https://youtu.be/_A5s6s6RvM).

fundamental task in algebraic geometry, 
  a branch of pure mathematics. This process involves isolating the intersection points 
  (or solutions) of multiple polynomials within a complex plane. Advances in computer 
  science, particularly algebraic geometry, have led to the development of various 
  algorithms for finding these intersection points since the 1960s. 
  Another method using a novel approach based on a constraint language framework is 
  presented in this work. This approach involves translating the problem of finding 
  intersection points into a constraint problem and using an existing algorithm to 
  solve it. Various existing algorithms for finding intersection points are first 
  reviewed, and a new constraint language framework for this task is then 
  developed. Compared to other methods, this approach is shown to be either more 
  efficient or feasible when using a currently known algorithm. This approach 
  is particularly adaptable to use with satisfiability problems and can be applied 
  more broadly to other problems within computer science. Finally, an implementation 
  of this approach in a practical context is described. 
  Results from testing this approach on a large dataset of benchmark problems are 
  presented and analyzed, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency for 
  finding intersection points in systems of polynomial equations. This approach 
  is shown to be capable of consistently and efficiently solving previously intractable 
  systems of polynomial equations with hundreds of variables. This approach 
  is particularly valuable because it allows for solving more complex systems of 
  polynomial equations and can be applied to other problems within computer science. 
  Additionally, it has the potential to contribute to theoretical developments in 
  algebraic geometry, particularly in the area of algorithmic problem solving. 
  Finally, it is suggested that this approach can be extended and applied to 
  solving multivariate systems of polynomial inequalities, which is a more 
  challenging task that requires further investigation and innovation. 
  Some open questions and challenges in this area are identified and highlighted. 
  Overall, it is hoped that these results and developments will be useful and 
  beneficial to future researchers in this field.

of various distributed problems and their relationships via the message efficiency of a distributed algorithm.  The efficiency, denoted as $E$, measures the number of rounds needed to solve a problem where each round represents a time interval in which nodes can exchange information, making it a crucial factor in designing efficient distributed protocols.  By investigating the one-message efficient problems, we demonstrate that determining the binary vector majority in a $\Delta$-anonymous broadcast channel can be solved with high efficiency, and further derive upper bounds for problems with specific broadcast channels, including $\Delta$-anonymous and broadcast error-correction.  Conversely, we show that maintaining binary vectors in fully anonymous and binary broadcast channels requires low but not one-message efficient solutions.  Additionally, we establish a new lower bound for the binary vector majority problem in directed graphs and improve existing bounds for flood routing, broadcast error-correction, and maintaining binary vectors in directed and anonymous broadcast channels. These statistics are typically calculated using oracle wordings, bypassing the ASR decoding process. For more precise benchmarks, including those for deep learning ASR systems, we need to integrate decoding into the evaluation process. This paper focuses on the Hiero hierarchical edit distance used to calculate WER, exploring two key aspects that influence ASR robustness benchmarks: word segmentation and tagging. We examine the impact of different segmentation and tagging schemes on the Hiero edit distance, analyzing the resulting variability. Our analysis shows that the most common word segmentation scheme in ASR robustness evaluation, which treats the word as a non-divisible segment, significantly increases the edit distance compared to more accurate schemes that account for word divisions. Furthermore, the tagging scheme's effect on the edit distance is also substantial, especially when tags indicate word beginnings or ends, as the Hiero algorithm is sensitive to these tags. To minimize bias in ASR robustness evaluation, we advocate for more detailed word segmentation and tagging protocols, taking into account the diverse applications of ASR systems. By providing theoretical and empirical analyses, as well as a set of benchmark data, we demonstrate the significance of word divisions and tagging information in ASR robustness evaluation. Our research also compares the robustness of ASR systems under the standard scheme used in the Lattice-Matching decoding algorithm and the Hiero decoder incorporating a more refined word segmentation and tagging scheme, revealing the potential for improved performance with the later method. By promoting more informed ASR robustness evaluation, we can accelerate the development and testing of advanced speech recognition systems capable of handling complex word divisions and tagging schemes. the CoDaFun software has been released with several key enhancements.  This release expands on the functionality introduced in the previous versions, particularly in the areas of parameter estimation and model assessment.  Compared to the earlier versions, this update incorporates Resampling methods to address issues related to the bias and variability associated with maximum likelihood estimates.  Furthermore, it offers the capability to perform score tests and efficient reference parameter estimation, both of which facilitate a deeper understanding of the estimated models and enhance model assessment procedures.  Additionally, the software now includes the capability to estimate models with location and scale parameters for extreme value distributions.  These improvements are complemented by the introduction of new functions.  A detailed description of the software's features and installation information are available on the CoDaFun website, while a comprehensive guide outlining the algorithms and their implementation is published in a corresponding paper.  A supplementary paper also explores the application of the software's tools for model assessment.  Ultimately, the goal of the CoDaFun software is to provide a versatile toolset to facilitate a comprehensive analysis of the properties of codified data.  This involves addressing fundamental questions such as: what the underlying model is, what parameters it includes, and how reliable these estimates are.  The availability of the software version 1.6.0 can be found on the project's website (codafun.uv.es), while users can access the source code through the GitHub repository (github.com/uv-codafun/codafun).  Additionally, a Windows installer is also provided on the project's website.  The functionality of the software has been extensively validated using simulated data, the analysis of which is documented in a corresponding paper.  Specifically, this paper evaluates the performance of the software's tools for parameter estimation, model assessment, and order selection based on simulated codified data characterized by varying levels of noise.  The results of these simulations are presented in tables and through graphical summaries, which also include the coverage rates of the corresponding confidence intervals.  These evaluations are consistent with the recommendations outlined in the software's manual.  Ultimately, this study showcases the capabilities of the software to analyze codified data, which include heavy tailed distributions, circadian rhythms, and Poisson distributions with and without regulation. Our software, called VyVu, can calculate virtual corrections using various methodologies, such as the operator product expansion or direct parton scattering principles. By applying various approximation techniques, like soft or massless factorization or dimensionless factorization, VyVu can generate perturbative components of parton distribution functions up to any desired order. Furthermore, VyVu can also calculate virtual corrections to parton distribution functions at higher orders, such as to order α_s^4(pert). We have applied this calculation to nucleon structure functions and gluon distribution functions, as well as to charm and beauty distribution functions, at QCD order α_s^3, incorporating two-loop coefficients. Our calculations are compatible with standard parton distribution function evolution codes, such as HOPES, and can be used in conjunction with other specialized codes, such as MINNIE, to compute distribution functions from matrix elements. Our software is now publicly available via a GitHub repository, allowing for easy integration into other programs used in particle and nuclear physics research. The application of VyVu to the calculation of gluon corrections to DGLAP equations will be documented in an upcoming publication. In contrast to traditional adversarial and bandit learning problems, the uncertainties present in sequential decision-making tasks complicate the implementation of established solutions.  To address this challenge, a new approach is proposed, incorporating established decision-theoretic principles and reinforced learning methods to effectively handle uncertain decision-making scenarios.  The methodology is grounded in a probabilistic framework that models uncertainty in therapeutic outcomes and treatment compatibility, as well as in the predictive models used to forecast these outcomes.  Utilizing a reverse reinforcement learning formulation, the approach identifies the optimal sequential treatment policies that maximize patient benefits and minimize adverse effects, incorporating uncertainty into the decision-making process.  The approach integrates the optimal policies with the development of custom loss functions, enabling physicians to learn the optimal treatment sequences even when there is significant unpredictability in the data.  The methodology is supported by theoretical analysis and multiple evaluations on real-world therapeutic sequences, demonstrating its effectiveness in learning optimal uncertain decision-making policies across multiple domains. This research investigates how translation impacts the detection of plagiarism between texts. It examines three key factors: 1) whether source code plagiarism can be transferred, 2) the impact of translation types, and 3) whether specific translations affect detection. Our analysis is based on a large, experimental code dataset involving real-world translations from English to Spanish and reverse translations from Spanish to English. The findings reveal that source code plagiarism can indeed be transferred but is influenced by the subject area; certain translations increase the similarity between code segments, while others decrease it; and current plagiarism detection techniques can detect translated code but are outperformed by a novel, translation-aware algorithm. Invasive on decision rules that maintain consistency when state structure remains the same, invariance is more narrowly defined and thus easier to work with.  By demonstrating that any equivariant decision rule that exhibits 'predictive postdiction invariance' can also be regarded as invariant for decision-making criteria including the worst-case loss and the conditional expected loss, this study ultimately shows that postdiction invariance serves as a deciding factor for equivariance.  This finding is further illustrated through empirical analysis of decision-making criteria on a well-known sequential decision-making task.  As a result of this investigation, decision criteria that emphasize postdiction invariance may yield better performance in terms of overall fit.  Conversely, criteria that prioritize predictive invariance may lead to decision rules that are more robust to changes in the state structure.  Ultimately, this study highlights the importance of distinguishing between decision criteria based on predictive and postdiction invariance.  This distinction enables decision-makers to achieve more precise goals - namely, selecting criteria that result in sequential decisions that are predictive postditionally invariant and thus equivariant.  This research is relevant not only to the specific setting of this study, but also more broadly, as it demonstrates the value of distinguishing between decision criteria based on predictive and postdiction invariance across a range of complex decision-making tasks. This study examines the benefits and drawbacks of utilizing field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) as the underlying hardware platform for ANNs, in light of the emerging competition for bandwidth, known as the memory wall. plicating, modular hardware language that utilizes Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) technology. Employing a resource-sharing, reconfigurable architecture, FiLex embodies the principles of Conjoined Replication, allowing the system to adapt to various configurations with interchangeable hardware modules. The shown examples demonstrate the flexibility of FiLex in balancing computation efficiency and reconfigurability through different engine designs. Specifically, we showcase a multi-task system consisting of a Mooglib-based audio engine and a Chomskylib-based Turing Machine, both of which can be reconfigured into separate components or combined into a single module. The hardware architecture of FiLex is described using the VHDL hardware description language, with a corresponding software language (SiLex) utilized for instruction set definition and virtual machine design. SiLex builds upon the concept of stack-based computation originally seen in MESA, incorporating additional elements such as macro expansion and polymorphic function calls to enhance the expressiveness of the language. The described system can be reconfigured either at hardware level or software level, with the capability to replicate both its hardware and software components to achieve various goals. By allowing the selection of suited data structures with suitable algorithms, FiLex empowers the developer to make informed decisions regarding computation efficiency, reconfigurability, and other system characteristics. The presented framework serves as a highly adaptable tool for creating unique hardware systems, enabling rapid prototyping and board design with feature-rich hardware development boards. The sources and hardware/Software models mentioned above are available at https://github.com/nfeldmann/FiLex. This enables potential users to duplicate, replicate, and experiment with the system and its accompanying resources. By distributing the sources, we aim to facilitate a collaborative effort to analyze, modify, and improve the technical complexity of FiLex, ultimately making it more robust and feature-rich. This contribution represents a significant advancement in the field of hardware languages, marking a notable application of the principles of Conjoined Replication on FPGA boards. This research extends the amalgamation property to include structures with named elements, which can be thought of as coloured structures.  Specifically, the study focuses on the existence of unique homomorphisms between certain structured sets, where the structures involve both graph and mapping components.  For a given category with structures, a defined functor preserves certain structural properties.  By demonstrating that the existence of amalgamations is preserved under certain conditions in a continuous semantics setting, the research shows that the properties are equivalent to the properties of free algebras.  Moreover, the study establishes that the properties are axiomatic descriptions of categorical concepts such as algebraic theories and preserving and reflecting structures.  An important outcome of the research is the discovery of equivalent categories based on the properties of structures with named elements and structured sets.  The study also provides examples of categories that satisfy the properties of structures with named elements, which cannot be modelled using structured sets.  Finally, the research presents axiomatic descriptions of categories such as abelian categories and categories with structures, which are preserved and reflecting.  These descriptions demonstrate that categories with structures, which are preserved and reflecting, can model the properties of continuous semantics for any axiomatic category.  This research contributes to the existing literature by showing that categories with structures, which are preserved and reflecting, can be equivalently represented by continuous semantics.  This discovery expands our understanding of categories with structures, which can be equivalently represented by continuous semantics.  This research expands the existing theorems found in Research in the Semantics of Procedure and Process, which were published in 1991.  Furthermore, the research introduces new concepts and establishes connections between categories with structures, which can be equivalently represented by continuous semantics, and categorical concepts such as algebraic theories.  This research addresses several open issues and provides examples of categories with structures, which satisfy the properties of structures with named elements.  These examples demonstrate that certain categories with structures can be equivalently represented by continuous semantics settings.  The research outlines future research directions in the field. A issue with training classification networks has been their tendency to be influenced by certain data examples to the point of memorization, which can result in poor generalization when tested with new data.  A technique to combat this was introduced in the ArXNet paper in 2017 by achieving double accuracy gain on the MNIST dataset by combining a complex model with a simpler one.  A more recent study investigated how model complexity affects this phenomenon by using simple models, discovering that there is an optimal range of complexity where memorization leads to poor generalization.  A more detailed analysis was then performed to understand what characteristics of training sets cause this phenomenon, which revealed that data examples causing memorization are often misclassified by baseline models and correspond to edge cases in the dataset.  As a result, restricting access to such examples during training leads to improved generalization performance and confirms that there is an optimal range of complexity where this effect occurs.  Using this observation, a simple yet effective approach was developed to improve the robustness of complex models by preventing them from learning from vulnerable examples.  This approach provides, for each test sample, a confidence metric that reflects the model's likelihood of making a mistake due to memorization, which can be used to improve robustness by removing sensitive data examples from the training set.  A more extensive experiment demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach, which was further combined with techniques to improve robustness in the presence of adversarial examples, such as trading purity for uncertainty in likelihood-based methods.  As a result, the new approach supports the improvement of multiple robustness metrics simultaneously against three different types of attacks. This study investigates this low-dimensional quantum electrodynamic coupling more closely. Initially, the model is analyzed using perturbation theory, which indicates that the light and atomic states remain distinct.
