This work addresses a stabilization problem for a particular difference equation that compares raw material production levels with desired targets. The equation models a multi-partite graph where each node represents a variable, and connections between nodes indicate comparisons among different groups of variables. Assuming an equilibrium exists among the variables, we analyze the linear system resulting from solving the equilibrium equation and examine its stability under different node configurations, ultimately proving a condition for global stability in a particular graph structure. Conversely, we show that simply connecting all nodes in a complete graph does not guarantee global stability. An extension to our model allows for the comparison of ratios of variables, which we use to develop a distributed estimator for a system consisting of a chain of interconnected subsystems. The estimator is globally stable for a particular type of graph structure, and its stability is globally consistent when the connections are complete. Furthermore, we find that a condition for global stability in a linear system of equations in the realm of positive variables is analogous to a known condition in graph theory, and we explore the implications of this analogy. By assuming all nodes in the system are connected, we show that a system of equations with variables representing material amounts and ratios is globally solvable, and this result has implications for dynamic systems. An example illustrating the effectiveness of our model is provided. The model is also scalable, as evidenced by a simulation of a large system. Additionally, we propose a mechanism for dynamically reconfiguring the connections in the system and maintaining global stability, as well as a strategy for dynamically adjusting the parameters and maintaining global stability in the system. Finally, we show that a model of a simplified production process is globally stable when a particular condition is met and the connections are complete, and this result translates to a corresponding linear system. An experiment validating our model is described. The model's ability to handle multiple relationships among variables is highlighted through an example of a system with variables representing material amounts and ratios, as well as through simulations of a contact process and a model of a simplified calcium homeostasis system. An experiment validating our model is described. The paper concludes by outlining areas for future research and direction. To address these challenges, researchers have proposed techniques such as data augmentation and Mixture-of-Experts architecture in the hope of improving the reliability of ensemble members. We find that, for $k\ge 4$, and large enough $n$, if $p$ is less than or equal to the threshold value $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{k} \left(1-\frac{1}{p}\right)$, then a $k$-edge coloring exists for $K(n)$ that doesn't contain a complete subgraph $K_{p+1}$ all red, and, for smaller $p$, we find an exact description of the complete subgraph $K_{p+1}$ with red edges in a $k$-edge coloring of $K(n)$. We also investigate the related Ramsey-Turán problem for $K_{p+1}$ and obtain new upper and lower bounds in this context. Our calculations also reveal a conjecture related to the exponential behavior of the complete subgraph $K_{p+1}$ with red edges in a $k$-edge coloring of $K(n)$.   hindered by issues stemming from bias in the algorithms' training data.
  Researchers have devised multiple approaches to address this challenge, which
  can be categorized into two primary methodologies: sensitivity analysis and
  fairness constraint techniques. While fairness constraint methods directly aim to
  incorporate bias mitigation, sensitivity analysis initially evaluates and
  identifies the sources of bias before developing an effective strategy.
  This study focuses on sensitivity analysis, which involves determining the
  effect of data bias on ML algorithms without making broad assumptions about the
  data distribution. Unlike existing techniques that require complex probabilistic
  models or structured data, this new approach applies to all ML algorithms and
  types of data, including text, images, and raw data. To detect data bias,
  this methodology relies on the performance difference of ML algorithms when
  trained on biased data subsets. Moreover, this approach accurately pinpoints
  the subsets responsible for the observed performance disparities without
  making any assumptions about the data distribution. Finally, this method
  identifies subgroups within the data that exhibit significant performance shifts
  when subjected to biased data sections. To demonstrate its efficacy, this new
  approach is tested on actual data from Amazon Mechanical Turk for two complex
  datasets, including images from the ImageNet archive and text from unstructured
  sources, including product descriptions and sentiment analysis data. The
  results show that this novel approach effectively detects data bias, which
  could have a considerable impact on the performance of ML algorithms and their
  final predictions. Ultimately, this method showcases its practical utility
  through a proposed mechanism for mitigating data bias.  The implementation of
  this new approach is accessible at https://github.com/nandhuri/bias-detector. 
  This study presents a new framework for detecting data bias in real-world
  applications, which demonstrates the practical value of bias detection and

These models have been widely used due to their efficiency and effectiveness; however, concerns have been raised about their interpretability. Understanding the behavior and contribution of individual nodes or edges in GNNs is essential for achieving real-world complexity. To address this, a new family of GNN models called edge-gated graph neural networks (EGNNs) was introduced. In EGNNs, an edge-aware aggregation module processes graph data by considering the characteristics of individual edges, and an edge-gated propagation module determines the propagation coefficient for each edge. By incorporating learnable gating parameters, EGNNs enable the adaptive selection of information propagated between adjacent nodes, and between different nodes. By incorporating these novel modules, EGNNs demonstrate superior performance on four public benchmark datasets. Furthermore, experiments conducted to evaluate the interpretability of EGNNs revealed that they prioritize the adaptation of information based on edge characteristics rather than arbitrary proximity criteria, and that they enable the expression of node features through distant edge interactions. Notably, EGNNs achieved parallelized training without affecting model performance, and demonstrated a significant reduction (at least 10%) in both computational complexity and storage requirements compared to conventional GNNs on large graphs. Overall, the integration of adaptive edge-aware aggregation and propagation mechanisms in EGNNs offers a promising path forward for both high-accuracy and interpretable node representation learning in GNNs. While RDF triplestores and property graphs are often utilized for comparable tasks, they differ significantly in terms of data modeling, query languages, and performance capabilities.  Our research aims to bridge the knowledge gap between these two technologies by achieving fast and scalable results when querying data stored in both formats.  A newly proposed hybrid approach, called PG-RDF, allows for the integration of property graphs and RDF data within a unified system.  Through the implementation of efficient indexing and query execution mechanisms, PG-RDF enables native query support for both property graphs and RDF triples, in addition to a proposed hybrid query language.  Extensive performance experiments using real-world data sets have shown significant improvement in query execution times over existing combined query solutions.  Notably, query execution times with PG-RDF have often outperformed those of property graph and RDF solutions individually, yielding an average speedup of 1.9 and 2.3 times, respectively.  In various instances, query execution times become negligible to the human observer, thereby addressing a longstanding combination problem known as the "join order" issue.  Moreover, PG-RDF has shown potential for delivering efficient model checking results in the context of modal logic calculations.  Our research outcomes suggest the feasibility and benefits of combining property graphs and RDF data in a single data management system.  Alongside the proposed approach and query language, our, implementation, and validated performance results are all made publicly available on GitHub for further use and exploration.  In particular, the integrated PG-RDF system and combined query language have been successfully incorporated into the OpenGraphDB open-source enterprise-level knowledge management system, enabling widespread application and impact in various domains and industries.   This paper introduces a novel approach to instruction tuning called
  SIBOL-Grad, which incorporates gradient-based optimization to refine model
  instructions. SIBOL-Grad operates by enhancing previously established SIBOL
  instructions through iterative refinement via gradient descent. Unlike
  prior approaches that rely on secondary objectives or constraint relaxation,
  SIBOL-Grad directly improves the accuracy of existing instructions on a
  task-specific dataset and thereby enhances performance on the original task
  without the need for additional hyperparameter adjustments. In addition, 
  SIBOL-Grad offers improved efficiency over other instruction tuning
  techniques, as it can be applied after just a few training iterations and 
  does not necessitate finetuning the underlying language model. Our experiments 
  validate the effectiveness of SIBOL-Grad on comprehension datasets that utilize 
  instructions, which can serve as a basic foundation for comprehension models 
  or are utilized as crucial components in multi-step reasoning models. SIBOL-Grad 
  demonstrates substantial potential in real-world applications by achieving qualitative 
  results on a complex question-answering task that involves understanding
  complex instructions for advanced Minimax decision-making in strategy games.  At 
  https://sibolgrad.github.io/, we have made our code and model datasets available 
  for the research community to utilize.  Our model architectures and training 
  scripts are also available for replication at

Absorption Fine Structure (XAFS) experiments have several key characteristics: they are biologically harmless, heavily absorbing materials that also contain elements with high XAFS sensitivity, and are available in a variety of pre-defined structures. Given the detection limitations of modern XAFS detectors, even trace amounts of these tracer particles can be easily overwhelmed by the primary sample's signal. As a result, accurate analysis of the tracer's contribution relies on sophisticated computational subtraction methods. To mitigate this issue, we suggest using spherical tracer particles with low density and coated with a thin layer of metal, significantly reducing their total absorption while keeping their XAFS signal intact. Using such a setup in computer simulations, we demonstrate that even a 5 micrometer thick low-density tracer layer, surrounded by a 2 nm thick metal coating, produces an XAFS signal that is not overwhelmed by the primary sample's signal, thus facilitating manual subtraction. Moreover, the proposed design yields an ideal condition in which the tracer's contribution has opposing phase and is significantly diminished relative to the primary sample's signal, thereby enhancing the accuracy of the subtraction procedure. This area of study is closely related to the foundational questions in complexity theory, particularly those surrounding logarithmic depth circuits. A key aspect of Dynamic Complexity involves demonstrating equivalences between complexity classes and symmetric-proc log-space (SP-SPACE) complexity classes, specifically by establishing equivalences between several depth-reductions and symmetric-proc log-space reductions. 

  This research focuses on two primary areas within Dynamic Complexity. Firstly, it investigates a hypothetical depth of log n circuit model and its influence on the completeness hierarchy. Secondly, it explores a complementary concept of 'unfolding' in log-space, and its relationship to deterministic transitive closure in O(log^2 n) depth. 

  A central result of this research shows that for every log-space predicate P, there exists a log n-depth circuit that solves P or its complement. This leads to two significant consequences. Firstly, it demonstrates that the complexity class SP-SPACE(log n) contains a complete predicate, enabling the construction of a high-complete predicate for the associated completeness hierarchy. Secondly, it shows that a transitive closure in O(log^2 n) depth cannot be further reduced to a log n-depth circuit, rectifying a previously established equivalence between transitive closure in SP-SPACE and polynomial-time version, namely TC ⊆ P. 

  An additional key result of this research indicates that a deterministic transitive closure in O(log^2 n) depth can be symmetrically reduced from any predicate in SP-SPACE(log n), leading to two further conclusions. Firstly, it shows that a log n-depth circuit model implies a symmetric-proc log-space model for deciding reachability in graphs.   In response, we introduce a novel method to assess a model's ability to withstand object variability.
  This method incorporates data from uncertain sources to create challenging scenarios for object categorization.
  By utilizing this approach, we can gauge a model's efficacy both generally and in specific situations, providing essential feedback for enhancing its architecture or training protocols. 
  Ultimately, we demonstrate the efficacy of our framework through its application to a straightforward image classification task. 
  In a basic experiment, we show that our method can effectively improve a model's performance by training it with data from uncertain sources, such as image tampering or deformation. 
  Specifically, by simulating the manipulation of a single object, we can increase a model's overall accuracy and its ability to correctly classify objects with manipulated appearances. 
  In addition, we found that our method not only improves a model's generalization but also its robustness against more complex and unpredictable transformations. 
  Therefore, we believe that our framework can serve as a starting point for developing theories and practical strategies for enhancing a model's adaptability and robustness. 
  By gauging a model's performance in challenging scenarios, we can uncover its inherent limitations and those of its training protocols, as well as discover novel inductive biases and heuristics. 
  In particular, we observed that a model trained with data from uncertain sources tends to exhibit the following behaviors: 
  It is more resilient to changes in the absence of category-level structure and less resistant to transformations with inherent structures not learned during training; 
  It is more effective at detecting stimuli that can easily be manipulated and is also more robust to changes in the presence of structures learned during training; 
  It is more productive but less efficient than a model trained in a homogeneous environment. 
  In light of these findings, we propose the use of data augmentation with uncertainty to improve a model's generalization and robustness. 
  In particular, we discovered that providing a model with random transformations can aid a model in: 
  Structuring its representation and reducing variability, thus making it less prone to changes in the absence of category-level structure; 
  Identifying and extracting key features from altered stimuli in the presence of structures not learned during training; 
  Developing decision-making heuristics that are both simple and complex, thus making it more productive but less efficient.

methods are explored as a class of methods that combine the advantages of Runge-Kutta and Volterra integrators.  Developing variance-reducing techniques for these methods is particularly challenging due to their non-Rankine structure in implicit stages.  This dissertation proposes a novel class of methods called Volterra-RK methods that efficiently tackle multivariate problems involving non-separable kernels, while maintaining the ability to apply local extrapolation techniques for enhanced efficiency.  By structuring these methods in a specific way, implicit stages can be reinterpreted as Volterra integrals, allowing for the application of Green's tensor or matrix decomposition in complex kernel combinations.  This innovative approach allows for the construction of high-order Volterra-RK methods with properties similar to those of traditional Runge-Kutta methods.  What's more, this formulation facilitates the creation of sparse schemes for systems involving large systems of multivariate non-separable kernels.  One such method, the fourth-order Volterra-RK method, is developed and analyzed in detail.  When applied to a previously stochastic problem that was previously intractable, it is now feasible to achieve a high degree of integration error reduction, specifically a decrease of a factor of 1048 compared to its traditional counterpart.  Furthermore, this dissertation also addresses implementation challenges, such as generating dense advantage tensors and approximating the inverse of the Jacobian matrix in complex systems.  Several efficient algorithms are proposed to tackle these issues, resulting in a significant reduction in computational cost.  The application of these methods to a variety of numerical test problems, as well as several stochastic problems that were previously intractable, demonstrates first-order and high-order convergence.  What's more, it achieves tighter bounds on integration error than its traditional counterpart, resulting in a reduction of a factor of 1048 compared to its traditional counterpart.  Ultimately, this innovative class of methods provides a solution to an enduring problem in the numerical integration of stochastic ODEs, opening up new avenues of research.  One potential area of exploration is the application of fEXTR in the Volterra-RK method to enhance its efficiency, as validated in various numerical test cases.  Another area of research involves developing control variate techniques that can be applied to the Volterra-RK method, as proven in various numerical test cases where it achieves a reduction of a factor of 1048 compared to its traditional counterpart.  Lastly, this innovative class of methods may be extended to tackle multivariate high-dimensional problems by developing sparse advantage tensors, as validated in various numerical test cases

has been proposed as a solution to the strong CP problem and has been heavily considered as a possible explanation for observed excess phenomena at the LHC and in cosmic rays.  As a result, numerous studies have been conducted to investigate the potential for production of these particles at hadron colliders through the decay of black holes.  This work updates those findings, using more recent BSM physics guidelines from the LHC Experiment Task Force, and focuses on two main scenarios:  one in which the axion couples to a top quark and another where it couples to a photon.  In the first case, significant production is possible only if the axion has a mass less than 500 GeV, but this scenario is subject to constraints from studies of color triality.  In the second case, significant production is possible only if the axion has a mass less than 100 GeV and also that it couples strongly to a photon, but this scenario is subject to constraints from studies of electroweak precision.  As a result, we conclude that a 3 TeV mass limit can be imposed on axions based on a simple model of black hole creation and decay.  This limit may be elevated to a 6 TeV mass limit if the initial state resonance of the black hole is possible at 100 GeV mass range for the axion.  The proposed LHC upgrade will further elevate this limit to a 16 TeV mass limit.  Finally, we note that these mass limits can be compromised if the axion is involved in the decay of new states beyond the standard model.  Therefore, we suggest that future LHC experiments should search for the axion through black hole creation and one of two possible processes, either top quark or photon production.  This search is feasible even if the axion is involved in the decay of new states beyond the standard model.  The proposed searches should be capable of setting the most stringent production limits at the LHC, possibly even reaching the region of coupling to a photon.  The proposed searches should be initiated as soon as possible and should be conducted as soon as possible with the current LHC data.  This proposal for a search strategy is suitable for 13 TeV and higher energy LHC experiments. Employing a multi-dimensional Bayesian approach with Markov chain Monte Carlo reporting the 1$\sigma$ confidence intervals, we found in the Boulder site's background measurements there is evidence for three-component decay patterns, with one of the components indicating an enhanced $^{220}$Rn content greater than its parent $^{228}$Th equivalent, and additional background components need to be accounted for to achieve optimal fit results.  The extracted parameters from the three-dimensional analysis match those obtained from frequency spectrum analysis, and our results imply the presence of additional geological components influencing the Boulder's ultra-low background measurements, predominantly dictated by the $^{220}$Rn component.  The approach and findings provide a background strategy for analyzing deep-site background measurements, and offer an alternative to traditional frequency spectrum analysis.  Furthermore, given the compatibility with the currently available data, this three-dimensional approach can be expanded to analyze measurements taken in Boulder's cavern, once published in an appropriate context.  The code utilized for the analysis is publicly accessible on GitHub at the address https://github.com/uBOULder/3DAnalysis.  We hope that these results can contribute to promoting research in the field of deep-site geochemical background measurements. **Numerical Algorithm Description**

Given an initial condition, the proposed algorithm generates a solution for the corresponding Riemann problem. This approach is based on the Chapman-Jouguet condition and involves the following main steps:

1.  **Initial Setup** - Divide the phase plane into a cell (A to C and D to B) based on the slope of the flexibility function.
2.  **Streamline Generation** - For each cell, calculate the speed of the shock/entropy-outgoing wave and the acceleration potential lines (E and F) across the cell boundary.
3.  **Wave Placement** - Place a shock/entropy-outgoing wave at the intersection of a potential line and the cell boundary, provided it matches the cell's speed and direction.
4.	**Update Cell Map** - Reflect the cell boundary based on the placed wave and update the adjacent cells.
5.	**Compute State** - For each cell, the state is computed using entropy-admitted waves.
6.	**Time March** - Based on the cell map, update time and repeat the process.
7.	**Check Convergence** - For entropy-admitted waves, check for convergence towards the broad weak solution.

**Code Implementation**

The code for the algorithm is written in C++ and is compatible with the Eigen library. It includes three distinct classes: `CellMap`, `Wave`, and `Streamline`, along with relevant constructor and member function implementations.

  Our research focuses on the problem of accurately determining an object's proximity (or influence area) while adhering to DP data release standards.  We initiate our investigation by formulating two practical scenarios: dispatching ambulances to incidents based on distance and determining the number of objects within a defined distance of each other (or proximity distribution).

  To address these challenges, we evaluate existing point process models (independent and identically distributed, Poisson gap, and truncated Poisson) under DP conditions and measure their statistical accuracy relative to their non-DP counterparts.

  Our analysis shows that among the evaluated models, the Poisson process achieves the highest level of accuracy with minimal deviation from its DP counterpart when considering proximity distributions.  However, its error accumulation hinders its practical application in dispatching ambulances, prompting us to propose a variant: the graduated Poisson process.

  Our findings demonstrate that when incorporating an extra parameter into the Poisson process, its statistical accuracy improves while reducing dispatching errors, bringing it closer to its DP counterpart.  Furthermore, by analyzing two datasets, we demonstrate that modifying the graduated Poisson process using DP data release can reduce dispatching errors by up to a factor of $\frac{e^{\lambda}}{2}$. the occurrence of hydra patterns in a reaction-diffusion model incorporating two distinct types of hydra enzymes, represented as $u$ and $v$, which interact with a signal molecule $w$.  Through a stability analysis on the attractor where the system reaches equilibrium, we demonstrate that the dynamic system is stable if both $u$ and $v$ decrease simultaneously and also when either $u$ or $v$ decreases alone while $w$ remains constant.  By applying a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods, we analyze the resulting nonlinear system and derive conditions under which the hydra pattern is localized or global, including the influence of parameter $\gamma$, which represents the signal molecule's diffusion coefficient.  Numerical solutions confirm our analytical findings and illustrate the dynamic transition between localized and global hydra patterns as the parameter $\gamma$ changes.  Ultimately, our analysis shows that the diffusion coefficient of the signal molecule is pivotal in the development and persistence of hydra patterns within this model.  This research highlights the utility of our approach for studying complex systems and illustrates the diverse behavior of the hydra model under varying diffusion coefficients.  This work also contributes to the ongoing discussion on strategy and diffusion in the evolution of spatial gene regulation. Despite advances in modeling large scale interconnected power systems, microgrid complexity is often oversimplified for ease of analysis, which could lead to inaccurate representations. This paper presents NaNNet, a straightforward, flexible, and performant algorithm for creating neural nets that can fit various binary classification problems within a specified radial influence area.  By utilizing NaNNet, researchers can create complex classification surfaces with minimal errors, even when competing with other neural nets.  This method relies on simple linear models and efficient optimization techniques, thereby avoiding complicated training procedures, and achieves fast training and prediction times.  NaNNet's key components include an efficient space partitioning method and a straightforward hyperparameter adjustment process.  Furthermore, NaNNet's code is compatible with scikit-learn, enabling easy integration and efficient performance.  Compared to other radial basis algorithms, NaNNet outperforms significantly, achieving up to a 90% reduction in prediction time while also simplifying the training process by minimizing the need for intricate hyperparameter adjustments and specialized data preprocessing.  NaNNet's successful application in radial basis algorithm contexts highlights its potential for resolving several longstanding issues, including inefficient prediction times and complicated hyperparameter selections, ultimately leading to a unified, user-friendly learning paradigm.  NaNNet's utility extends to solving complex regression problems, as demonstrated by the binary classification application in this study, and can be adapted for other tasks such as multi-class classification, constant prediction, and time-series prediction, as well as data augmentation, latent variable detection, and anomaly prediction, making it a valuable tool for practitioners and researchers.  NaNNet's functionality is available at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/NaNNet for the purpose of research.  This paper has been formally accepted for publication in Knowledge-Based Systems, Volume 242, 2021, following a rigorous review process.  NaNNet's related work, including algorithm details, can be found at https://indigopurple.github.io/NANNet/, as well as information on data sets, experiments, and reproducibility. text analysis can be distillated into a single, unified concept. The first technique, typically associated with statistical linguistics, involves measuring word importance within a narrow context by counting co-occurrences. The second technique, commonly employed in deep learning applications, involves using a pre-trained neural network to assign each word a fixed-dimensional vector representation that incorporates contextual information. A fundamental challenge in analyzing text using vector representations is addressing contextual variability - capturing a word's consistent, underlying features despite varying contexts. We discover that this challenge can be successfully resolved by integrating the methods from both techniques, resulting in context-aware representations that incorporate both global characteristics and local nuances. Notably, our findings indicate that neural network-generated word vectors are inherently compatible with statistical linguistics' importance metrics, paving the way for a more unified text analysis framework that incorporates the strengths of both approaches. Notably, our results are consistent across six widely-used text corpora and three state-of-the-art neural network architectures, demonstrating the robustness of this unified concept. By integrating the methods of both techniques, we are able to provide a more comprehensive explanation of how word meanings evolve dynamically over the course of a given text passage - a predictive model that significantly outperforms existing models and has practical applications in both augmented human intelligence and the development of more sophisticated automated systems for text analysis. A supplementary website contains additional details regarding our research and the accompanying code, along with the results of our experiments in raw format. By publishing our research in this paper, we aim to provide a clear roadmap for researchers on how to implement this unified concept, incorporating both techniques, to analyze text effectively. Invariance of the $sp(4)$ algebra allows us to switch between kicked top and qutrit systems. The corresponding quantum phase transition in a 2D lattice model is investigated, revealing an interesting correlation between phase transition point and algebraic invariants. The origin of this correlation lies in the nonlinear quantum dynamics' dependence on the semisymmetric state's quantum dimension. This demonstrates how algebraic invariants can be used to study phase transitions in large systems. Furthermore, we propose a quantum state-dependent non-unitary evolution model as a new approach to engineering phase transitions. The model exhibits a complete phase transition in a 1D lattice system and the transition point can be controlled by adjusting a nonlinear evolution coefficient. The study of phase transitions in nonlinear quantum systems opens up new avenues for research and provides a framework for studying quantum critical phenomena. The model can be applied to systems like the kicked qutrit and qudit systems as well as lattice models. The approach can be extended to other types of phase transitions. By applying a bending energy metric, the network's topology can be characterized in terms of curvature. When this energy decreases, the network's hierarchy becomes more uniform, resulting in fewer distinct curvature levels and a shift towards lower curvature values. Conversely, an increase in bending energy leads to a more fragmented and diverse hierarchical structure consisting of multiple curvature levels. Our research reveals that a network's ability to store and process information over time is directly linked to its capacity for displaying rapid and sustained oscillations. Specifically, the condition for supporting these oscillations is met when the curvature levels exhibit a particular ordered sequence, an observation that provides an alternative explanation for the storage capability based solely on the network's curved structure. By examining the effects of random perturbations on curved hierarchical networks, we have identified two distinct types of long-lasting transient states characterized by different patterns of curvature distribution. Moreover, we have observed that an abrupt shift in the curve hierarchy, known as curvature avalanche, plays a crucial role in the dynamics of these transient states and found that it can be triggered by specific curvature transitions at the edge of the network. By tracing the anisotropic spread of curvature avalanches, we have gained insight into the direction-dependent influence of curvature transitions on the network's dynamics. Our study also reveals that the stability of curvature avalanches is directly linked to the network's hierarchical structure and the distribution of curvature values. Numerical simulations have been complemented by theoretical results showing that in a curved hierarchical network, the distribution of curvature avalanches can be classified into two types: one characterized by unidirectional curvature spread and the other by bidirectional spread. The findings of our research suggest that it is possible to read out the information stored in the curve hierarchy by identifying specific locations of curvature transitions and by analyzing the direction-dependent spread of curvature avalanches. The concept of reading out the information is most feasible in cases where bidirectional avalanches occur and the distribution of curvature values at the edge of the network is uniform. At least one such reading-out strategy is developed and demonstrated for a curved hierarchical network. The present work is a development of the research contained within the article published under the same title in Nature Communications, \textbf{9}, 2223, 2018. A detailed analysis has been added of the types of long-lasting transient states, characterized by different patterns of curvature distribution, and the associated mechanisms of curvature spread.   For trees, we provide a simple $+O(\log \Delta)$-round algorithm that uses minimal communication, improving upon previous strategies that relied on more complex communication.

We introduce the "public path" approach, enabling the communication of critical information in specific hop-limited networks to facilitate consensus.

Stramzki discovered a connection between Carlsson's theorem and a combination of the Steenrod operation behavior under transposition and the atomicity of the top Steenrod operator. This correspondence held for odd prime p and used $\Lambda$-coalgebra techniques. Our work demonstrates that this relationship can be expressed more simply using key $\Lambda$-coalgebra properties along with the descent correspondence for square-zero algebras, without relying on transposition. This approach reveals a broader significance, showing that the atomicity of the top Steenrod operator is a consequence of the properties of the Hopf algebra itself, and that this atomicity is associated with copermutative comalgebras. Additionally, our research introduces square-zero algebras and descents of comalgebras in the general context of Hopf algebras, and identifies a limit process that yields the May chain. This process can be expressed as taking a square-zero algebra's descent and then its limit, as compared to the traditional method of first taking the limit of the comalgebra and then its descent. Our research also generates a new interpretation of the May chain through the filter degree of square-zero algebras, and demonstrates that this degree is an essential component of the degree of the May chain. Finally, our research shows that the filter degree of the May chain can be equated with the degree of the $\Lambda$-coalgebra Lyshchynsky operator, as defined by Miller and Schenck. This equivalence, along with previously noted connections, generates several degree-related theorems. For instance, when the degree of the May chain is p, it indicates that $H_p(X)$ is p-local and $p$-connective. This finding is consistent with earlier work by Napolitani and Zarzisky on $p$-connective Hopf algebras. Our research also shows that the degree of the May chain is p if and only if $\mathcal{A}_p(X)$ is a graded $p$-local algebra, and proves that the degree of the May chain is 2 when $X$ is 2-connected. Furthermore, our research reveals that the degree of the May chain is 2 if and only if $H_2(X)$ generates $H_p(X)$. Our most significant contribution, however, is the discovery that the degree of the May chain can be expressed as the degree of the $\Lambda$-coalgebra Lyshchynsky operator, as mentioned above.

A different material, the doped boron trisulfide (BTS) cluster, has been studying the behavior of BTS through first-principles calculations.  A notable distinction exists between BTS and graphene, as BTS exhibits multiple possible ground states that shift in response to pressure, unlike single-layer graphene which only exhibits one ground state under all conditions.  A phase transition from a C2v symmetric rhombohedral structure to a higher-symmetry C4v cubic structure occurs at around 45 GPa, and this transformation is characterized by the formation of bond between sulfur atoms at higher pressures.  Calculations indicate BTS in its cubic form at 60 GPa exhibits some similarities with phase-shifted graphene, yet key characteristics remain distinct.  A predicted pressure-induced metal-insulator phase transition within BTS at around 20 GPa is confirmed, and it is observed that bond length within the material remains relatively constant at both pressures of 20 and 60 GPa.  A predicted tendency for self-organization within BTS material has also been found, as well as pressure-induced formation of possible adsorption sites at surface.  These findings have significant implications for understanding quantum phase transitions within materials with complex bonding, and potential uses for pressure-induced transformation in adsorption studies. Typically, CT scans provide detailed images but require specialized software to interpret them.  Meanwhile, radiologists make clinical decisions based on visual inspections of slice images, implying that sufficient information lies within these images for clinical use. However, our research found that using convolutional layers in 2D images is suboptimal compared to a simple model, and that combining multiple slice images in a single 3D block provides valuable features for classifying lung segments as normal or abnormal. which encompass both bright and dim conditions, pose a challenge to rendering realistic scenes.  The problem is addressed by using two methods to capture and reconstruct HDR environments in realistic and efficient ways.  Firstly, a neural patch-based synthesis approach predicts an approximate HDR environment based on a set of learned patch samples.  Secondly, a refinement technique utilizes RGBD data from common consumer devices to produce a final HDR environment through analysis and rendering.  By combining these methods, we achieve accurate HDR environment map recreation from synthetic data, also validating the results across two widely used rendering engines in the gaming industry.  The achieved results demonstrate the potential of our technique to enable the creation and rendering of more realistic HDR environments in virtual reality applications.  The associated code and dataset will be publicly available for further research and development.  The proposed technique offers benefits in terms of computational speed, accommodating various HDR compression formats, and enabling the incorporation of synthetic data in VR environment mapping applications.  The contribution of our work beyond existing solutions in HDR environment mapping lies in its focus on a more comprehensive and realistic approach, and its potential to facilitate more accurate semantic segmentation and recurrent shape synthesis scenarios in computer vision.  The novel technique has been demonstrated to improve scene realism and achieve compatible rendering times, also addressing known biases in previous HDR environment mapping methods by incorporating analytic Refine stages to produce more diverse and synthetic results.  The potential of our technique to be adapted in real-world applications is also explored, and the work remains versatile to be further extended and developed upon, also including new directions in research for future work.
